Photograph: Everett/Shutterstock Movies Review Rule Breakers review – rousingly feelgood real life story of Afghan girls’ robotics team This story of emancipated young women escaping draconian social strictures brims with enthusiasm and features a cameo from Phoebe Waller-Bridge Phuong Le Mon 17 Nov 2025 02.00 EST Last modified on Mon 17 Nov 2025 02.02 EST Share B ased on a true story, Bill Guttentag’s rousing drama attests to the resilience of women who dare to dream despite draconian social strictures. The film follows Roya Mahboob (Nikohl Boosheri), a trailblazing coach and businesswoman in Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) who assembles a robotics team of Afghan girls for international competitions. The young dreamers hail from different walks of life but they all share the same zest for engineering. They face the same dangers too; in a country where women are not encouraged or even allowed to pursue higher levels of education, their quest for medals sees opposition from their own families as well as public scorn from conservatives. Rule Breakers is at its most thrilling during the competition sequences, which splice together real-life documentary footage of the events with fictional re-enactments. (There’s even an appearance from Phoebe Waller-Bridge as a host.) A breathless enthusiasm thrums through the film, as the camera swirls around the young competitors, all energised by their love for science. These spaces are portrayed as a haven that encourages camaraderie rather than competitiveness, and in a world divided by military conflicts and war, they offer a utopiian vision of international collaboration and solidarity. When it comes to the darker aspects of the story, though, Rule Breakers is less assured. Except for minor scenes depicting the girls’ rejection for American visas, the film rarely grapples with the war in Afghanistan and its effects on women. From external funding to newspaper coverage, the film sets up a dichotomy between western support and domestic oppression, but this is a distinction that requires more political nuance considering the legacy of American interventionism in the region. While spirited in parts, the journey taken by this extraordinary robotics team deserves a more layered storytelling approach than that of a feelgood movie. Rule Breakers is on digital platforms from 17 November. While these series have never been afraid to touch on difficult topics, they are more defined by their tonal lightness and their breezy sense of humor. While plenty of series have defied this status quo, some series that are particularly interesting to analyze are the ones that changed their style throughout their run. Ranging from captivating, character-led crime-comedies to arresting feats of adult animation, and even to some of the genre’s most iconic series, these six shows made the drastic decision to turn down a far darker route heading into their final seasons. In some cases, the pivot works an absolute treat, leading to enriched and engaging finales that have become unforgettable highlights of the form. Other cases were disastrous missteps that distanced fans from their favorite characters at a crucial point in the story. All of them are worth examining to see how and why the creators attempted so dramatic a turn so late in the piece. 5 \'Arrested Development\' (2003–2019) Michael Bluth (Jason Bateman) makes a pose while talking as Tobias Funke (David Cross) mocks him by mimicking his stance in \'Arrested Development\' Season 5 (2019). Netflix Arrested Development certainly had a stagnated run throughout its five-season tenure, with its first three seasons coming out in three consecutive years before Netflix launched a Season 4 revival in 2013 and then another revival in the form of its fifth and final season in 2019. Across this tumultuous and sporadic release schedule, the hit comedy series follows the Bluths, a dysfunctional family of eccentric and borderline insane individuals who find the wealth that facilitates their spoiled lifestyles suddenly evaporate when the family patriarch and successful businessman George Bluth Sr. ( Jeffrey Tambor ) is imprisoned for fraud. Responsibility for managing the family falls to Michael Bluth ( Jason Bateman ), the only sensible member of the family, whose efforts to do the right thing and keep everyone united usually face obstacles in the form of his relatives’ materialistic, selfish, and juvenile ways. Where the first three seasons operated with a sense of lovable redemption for the miscreant mob, Arrested Development ’s two revivals had a crueler, more cutting nature. While it was a minor issue in Season 4, the shift became overbearing in the fifth and final season of the series, conjuring not only a greater sense of moral depravity through its emphasis on the characters’ unedifying flaws, but an unfortunate whiff of curt joylessness as well. The series always flaunted a certain irreverence, but Arrested Development Season 5 overplays its hand, presumably in an effort to remain fresh and surprising, but it only succeeds in losing the magic of its earlier seasons, creating an unrecognizable and unrewarding mess from what was once a razor-sharp comedy . 4 \'Fleabag\' (2016–2019) Phoebe Waller-Bridge staring into the camera while sitting in a pew in \'Fleabag\' Season 2. Image via Prime Video Given Fleabag consists of just two seasons and twelve episodes in total, it is staggering to fathom the scale of the cultural impact it has had. It is also quite perplexing to consider how the series changes quite substantially from Season 1 to Season 2 while remaining true to its core values and still delivering on the absorbing balance of razor-sharp comedy targeting everyday life and the underlying drama and despair of the titular character. The British comedy-drama follows a dry-witted and depressed woman known only as Fleabag ( Phoebe Waller-Bridge ) as she navigates life and love in the whirlwind that is modern-day London, as she struggles to overcome her feelings of grief and guilt regarding the death of her best friend, all while distancing herself from anyone who tries to help her process her emotions. While both seasons maintain plenty of comedy and drama, Season 2 is noticeably darker, delving into Fleabag’s complex emotional journey with a greater sense of urgency and honesty as she gradually grows beyond her despair as her unlikely friendship with the Hot Priest ( Andrew Scott ) starts to materialize into love. The season’s increased bleakness is a wonderful byproduct of its greater depth . It builds upon the richness of the first season magnificently to deliver a resolution to the story that is bittersweet but gorgeously cathartic. As both star and screenwriter, Waller-Bridge makes it work phenomenally, creating a series of unbelievable emotional range—given its relatively brief run—that stands as one of the defining small-screen triumphs of the 2010s , and an astute marriage of comedy and drama that is truly flawless from start to finish. 3 \'M*A*S*H\' (1972–1983) The M*A*S*H crew hugging and saying goodbye in the final episode, "Goodbye, Farewell and Amen" Image via CBS One of the more iconic series, not only in the context of comedy television but in the history of small-screen entertainment, M*A*S*H famously follows the medics at a Mobile Army Surgical Hospital during the Korean War, exhibiting how they use humor as a coping mechanism as they confront the horrific effects of battle. Based on Robert Altman ’s black comedy film of the same name from 1970, the hit series was never shy of using its wartime setting to address the severity of conflict, and it even has several episodes that are famous for their upsetting lulls. The last season, however, showcases a greater commitment to examining the brutality of war and pivots from outright comedy to a more concentrated war weariness at times as a result. Perhaps the best instance of this comes in the series’ finale, “Goodbye, Farewell, and Amen,” as the usually irreverent jokester Hawkeye Pierce ( Alan Alda ), being treated in a psychiatric hospital following a nervous breakdown, recalls an incident on a bus when his insistence that a refugee keeps her baby quiet to avoid detection from an enemy patrol leads to her smothering her child. It is a harrowing passage that illustrates how much bolder and bleaker the series was willing to go compared to the earlier seasons of its 11-season run. The increased drama is widely regarded to be a masterstroke, one that ensured M*A*S*H remained dynamic throughout all of its 256 episodes right up until its glorious two-hour finale that remains the most-watched single episode of any series in America. 2 \'Barry\' (2018–2023) A stressed and dejected looking Barry Berkman (Bill Hader) stands in a black t-shirt in \'Barry\' (2018-2023). HBO As a black comedy crime show following Barry Berkman ( Bill Hader ), a former U.S. Marine suffering from PTSD, as he finds an unlikely passion for acting while working as a hitman, Barry always flaunted a healthy dose of dramatic heft throughout its first three seasons, even if its beginnings are renowned more for their unique comical premise rather than their philosophical ponderings. The series did become increasingly dark as it went on, though, with Hader and co-creator Alec Berg becoming bolder at experimenting with the reliable mixture of dark humor and ultra-violence by introducing whiffs of real human drama to the fold. This balancing act takes a distinct elevation in intensity in Barry’s fourth and final season, with Barry in prison for murder and working to broker a deal with the FBI to work as an informant in exchange for a reduced sentence. The endearing quirkiness of Barry ’s situation in earlier seasons evaporates, with Season 4 committing to realizing the character as a vicious and volatile vessel of self-loathing whose outbursts of extreme violence are treated with an enhanced dramatic brutality compared to the absurdist, morbidly comical slant his actions were presented with in prior seasons. The unexpected tonal shift wasn’t necessarily met with universal appreciation from the fanbase, many of whom felt the show’s drastic change of mood correlated with weaker writing and less impactful narratives, but critics welcomed the evolution of the story as a daring way to wrap up the series. 1 \'BoJack Horseman\' (2014–2020) A scruffy and weathered looking BoJack Horseman stands on a bridge at night, the full moon serving as his backdrop as he talks on the phone in \'BoJack Horseman\' (2014-2020). Netflix Not dissimilar to Barry , BoJack Horseman is a series that always toed the line between laugh-out-loud hysterics and poignant, blindsiding drama. The groundbreaking Netflix adult animation follows BoJack Horseman ( Will Arnett ), a television actor who made his name in a hit family sitcom in the \'90s, who has since fallen into a cyclical lifestyle of addiction, self-loathing, and dreams of a second chance in the limelight while living as a washed-up celebrity in Los Angeles. Between attempts to launch a career comeback that will garner him artistic accolades and self-destructive benders that dismantle his chances of happiness and success, BoJack’s tendency to make mistakes and irrational decisions that harm those around him, a point that becomes painfully relevant in the series’ sixth season. Regret, consequences, and the lingering effects of trauma all become focal points of the final season, and while many would rightfully argue that those themes had been prevalent since the beginning of BoJack Horseman , the final episodes’ endeavor to address them more directly ensures the series takes on a distinctly different tone than its earlier seasons. It is an evolution that is handled magnificently, with the series’ darkening tone coinciding with BoJack’s long-standing internal turmoils surfacing in the most devastating and humiliating ways possible. The comedy, while still outrageously absurd, is steeped in tragedy . "/> ‘Fleabag’ is a reminder that love will pass, probably Katie Hulse | Staff Katie Hulse Author email Nov 6, 2025 Nov 6, 2025 Comments Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Chloe Kim | Senior Staff Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Love is heavy. Like an excruciating mound of weight on your back. A million pounds that you lug around that, as you try to heave it off the ground, inevitably drags you back toward it. It is embarrassing and horrific and also universally coveted. As I have been revisiting the concept of “art as a time machine” every week, it feels pointless to write about art without confronting the difficult truth that love is its most relentless subject matter. It seems to be indubitably trivial to study the way that time changes media without exploring how love changes art. “Fleabag,” created by, written by and starring Phoebe Waller-Bridge, is a piece of art that changed for me after I underwent the humiliation ritual of falling in love. I used to carefully strain out the cheesy, tasteless art in my life, sculpting a fortress of highbrow media around myself. But it’s been dreadful to learn that when you’re in love — like, really in love — you forget about your highbrow standards. The songs no longer make me wince; instead, they make sense. The rain falls quieter. Clothes are lighter on your skin, and then, as you allow yourself closer to the storm of love, they hang heavy and drenched. I used to spend my life wielding umbrellas and waterproof jackets to protect myself from the torrents of love. But now, I find myself bare in its downpour. I take delight in those cheesy songs. And for the first time, I understand overdone proclamations of love in movies and TV shows. “Fleabag”has been one of my favorite TV shows for years — long before love — despite being the antithesis to any romantic feeling. In its second season, it is a love story between the main character, Fleabag, (Phoebe Waller-Bridge) and a priest. It is dry, witty, pessimistic and always waiting rabidly to harshly remind me: My emotions are mortal. At the climax of the story, the priest makes a speech at a wedding. I’ve always regarded it as merely beautiful and fitting, maybe a little overly mushy and most definitely not the truth. Now, I feel I have the privilege of understanding it fully. My father likes to watch this episode after anything disturbing or scary. He sees it as a return to humanity, or something like that. On my most recent rewatch with my family, I devoured the wedding speech in a way that was impossible before the relationship that I’m in now. In a way that helped me accept that love is agonizing but apparently worth feeling. The priest’s famous lines read, “It makes you doubt yourself, judge yourself, distance yourself from the other people in your life. It makes you selfish. It makes you creepy, makes you obsessed with your hair, makes you cruel, makes you say and do things you never thought you would do. It’s all any of us want, and it’s hell when we get there.” And while I do believe love is all of these things, I never thought it would make me see art so differently. A nourishing relationship comes with so many little sacrifices. These small forfeits accumulate quietly. Love isn’t just a feeling; it’s a commodity. It has invented value, and just like everything else, it does not come free. Emotional highs and lows drive some kind of invisible stock of connection. At love’s most fundamental, when you allow someone to get to know you, you’re eradicating the version of yourself that others once could know. And when you love that someone knows you so well, you shut out the rest of the world. But honestly, I would be lying if I tried to say love is something that could be logically measured or placed on a scale. Its value derives from its sickening irrationality, and when real decisions are forced upon love, sacrifices are often an afterthought. In “Fleabag,” the priest chronically sacrifices his religious beliefs for his opportunity at love. And in the end, the cost is too high. Abandoning our main character at a bus stop post-one-sided-love-confession, he promises Fleabag, “It’ll pass.” The phrase triumphs as the famous romantic certainty of the series: that love is all-consuming but also beatable. There are many versions of love and many places to invest it. The priest decides to invest his in religion. Whether due to religious responsibilities or predestined distance, people in love, at one time or another, must be forced to confront the unknown value of their relationship — forced to decide what exactly they are willing to sacrifice to sustain it. My significant other is, unfortunately, also my best friend. Soon, I will be forced to make impossible decisions about my illogical feelings. I am going to graduate and he is moving abroad. While we spend our days numbed by our own happiness, reality’s ugly head is already rearing. And while the dilemma is perhaps small, it feels bigger than any piece of art or media can solve. The concept of measuring relationships is something that has been weighing on my mind. I have been desperately attempting to be rational, to gain confidence in my malleability, attempting to fit something incomprehensible into a pros and cons list. And from an unbiased scribble of reason, it does not make sense to hold onto something as youthful, naive and content as my relationship. I keep telling myself that I could be anywhere in a year, while he remains here or somewhere else corrupting his soul in investment banking. Why would I want to stay with anyone in investment banking? Yet for some reason, I keep thinking about the line that Fleabag’s sister, Claire, says to Fleabag after the priest’s speech. She says, “The only person I’d run through an airport for is you.” But right after saying it, Claire chases someone else through an airport. Time is the only measurement slightly worthwhile to my relationship, but that’s only because I think that love itself is predicated on time. Some people spend it making art, and others spend it running through airports. He is the author of several novels and hosts the podcast Wanging On with Maria McErlane. Tony Lankester, chief executive of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society, said: “Our ambassadors represent the critical role the Fringe plays in the lives of so many who got their start on the stages of Edinburgh and, today, are at the top of their game in the world of the arts. “Welcoming Graham to the fold is a real pleasure – he is someone who exemplifies the joy and generosity of the Fringe spirit, unapologetically passionate about the arts and a huge advocate of the importance of the Fringe in his own career. “As an ambassador he will be uniquely positioned to help inspire the next generation of artists, and we’re excited to be working with him on this mission.” The Edinburgh Festival Fringe will run from August 7 to 31 next year. Graham Norton has said he is “delighted” to be the newest ambassador for the Edinburgh Festival Fringe – where he started his career as a comedian more than 30 years ago. Whatever the case, you’re on the hunt for something to binge-watch on Netflix this weekend, and we’ve got some recommendations. This week’s lineup of bingeable shows includes a new thriller that’s topping the Netflix charts, a hidden gem featuring “Wicked” star Jonathan Bailey and a beloved sitcom you might want to revisit before it leaves Netflix in December. “The Beast in Me” (2025) “The Beast in Me” (Netflix) It’s the No. 1 show on Netflix for a reason! Netflix’s new psychological thriller series stars Claire Danes as an acerbic, reclusive writer who’s removed herself from society, a shell of herself after the death of her son. She’s also no longer able to write … until a man accused of murdering his wife moves next door and sparks her imagination. Danes and co-star Matthew Rhys (who is especially committed and compelling) establish a fabulously crunchy, sticky, impossible-to-put-down dynamic between their two characters from the get-go, and the series wisely wastes no time putting its two prickly and unpredictable leads together in unexpected ways. A limited series mystery is always a go-to pick for a weekend binge-watch and “The Beast in Me” is one of the best of the genre this year. “Crashing” (2016) Phoebe Waller-Bridge in “Crashing” (Channel 4) If the arrival of “Wicked: For Good” has you in the mood for more Jonathan Bailey, there’s a lesser-known U.K. comedy series waiting for you on Netflix. Created by and starring Phoebe Waller-Bridge, “Crashing” is like a rowdier, hard-partying sister series to her TV masterwork, “Fleabag,” which premiered just a few months later in 2016. The series centers on six twenty-somethings who take advantage of cheap rent and cohabitate in a disused hospital, quickly becoming a messy tangle of friendships, frenemies, sexual tension and romance. A bit debauched but soulful and witty, “Crashing” is a perfect weekend binge since it’s just six episodes — just be warned, they go too fast and you’ll be sad when it’s over. 16:30 Irish actor Fiona Shaw received her first two Emmy nominations in 2019 – in the categories of Supporting Actress in a Drama Series for her role in Killing Eve, and Guest Actress in a Comedy Series for her role in Fleabag. The two performances were the result of a fruitful creative relationship with producer and actor Phoebe Waller-Bridge , who she describes as the “daughter I wish I’d had”. Speaking on The Irish Times Women’s Podcast, Shaw says that the Fleabag and Killing Eve creator is a “person who is full of life. She’s got much more confidence than I would ever have had at that age”. Shaw first worked with Waller-Bridge on her smash hit spy thriller Killing Eve in 2018 and tells podcast presenter Kathy Sheridan that the English star is, “really something else”. The pair collaborated again on Waller-Bridge’s tragicomedy Fleabag. However, the role almost didn’t happen, and only came about because the filming of Fleabag ran over which meant the Harry Potter star was available to do the role. “I was in the middle of doing Cendrillion at Glyndebourne, and I was directing it, and it’s a huge opera and I said, ‘I can’t do anything in your Fleabag, I just can’t’. And then weirdly, Christmas came and went, and she said, ‘We’ve overrun’.” Shaw particularly praised the screenwriter’s ability to rewrite scenes while starring in them, adding, “she can spin plates like nobody else”. The Cork star also discussed her latest film, Park Avenue, which features a fraught mother-daughter dynamic. In the film, Shaw bares all with a nude scene, of which she says she didn’t mind doing. “The team on it was quite a small team,” she says praising director Gaby Dellal and producer Diana Phillips. She goes on to say, “When you work with good people, as with these two, you do anything for them. “You don’t feel you’re exposing anything that you will regret. Photograph: Everett/Shutterstock Movies Review Rule Breakers review – rousingly feelgood real life story of Afghan girls’ robotics team This story of emancipated young women escaping draconian social strictures brims with enthusiasm and features a cameo from Phoebe Waller-Bridge Phuong Le Mon 17 Nov 2025 02.00 EST Last modified on Mon 17 Nov 2025 02.02 EST Share B ased on a true story, Bill Guttentag’s rousing drama attests to the resilience of women who dare to dream despite draconian social strictures. The film follows Roya Mahboob (Nikohl Boosheri), a trailblazing coach and businesswoman in Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) who assembles a robotics team of Afghan girls for international competitions. The young dreamers hail from different walks of life but they all share the same zest for engineering. They face the same dangers too; in a country where women are not encouraged or even allowed to pursue higher levels of education, their quest for medals sees opposition from their own families as well as public scorn from conservatives. Rule Breakers is at its most thrilling during the competition sequences, which splice together real-life documentary footage of the events with fictional re-enactments. (There’s even an appearance from Phoebe Waller-Bridge as a host.) A breathless enthusiasm thrums through the film, as the camera swirls around the young competitors, all energised by their love for science. These spaces are portrayed as a haven that encourages camaraderie rather than competitiveness, and in a world divided by military conflicts and war, they offer a utopiian vision of international collaboration and solidarity. When it comes to the darker aspects of the story, though, Rule Breakers is less assured. Except for minor scenes depicting the girls’ rejection for American visas, the film rarely grapples with the war in Afghanistan and its effects on women. From external funding to newspaper coverage, the film sets up a dichotomy between western support and domestic oppression, but this is a distinction that requires more political nuance considering the legacy of American interventionism in the region. While spirited in parts, the journey taken by this extraordinary robotics team deserves a more layered storytelling approach than that of a feelgood movie. Rule Breakers is on digital platforms from 17 November. While these series have never been afraid to touch on difficult topics, they are more defined by their tonal lightness and their breezy sense of humor. Ranging from captivating, character-led crime-comedies to arresting feats of adult animation, and even to some of the genre’s most iconic series, these six shows made the drastic decision to turn down a far darker route heading into their final seasons. In some cases, the pivot works an absolute treat, leading to enriched and engaging finales that have become unforgettable highlights of the form. Other cases were disastrous missteps that distanced fans from their favorite characters at a crucial point in the story. All of them are worth examining to see how and why the creators attempted so dramatic a turn so late in the piece. 5 \'Arrested Development\' (2003–2019) Michael Bluth (Jason Bateman) makes a pose while talking as Tobias Funke (David Cross) mocks him by mimicking his stance in \'Arrested Development\' Season 5 (2019). Netflix Arrested Development certainly had a stagnated run throughout its five-season tenure, with its first three seasons coming out in three consecutive years before Netflix launched a Season 4 revival in 2013 and then another revival in the form of its fifth and final season in 2019. Across this tumultuous and sporadic release schedule, the hit comedy series follows the Bluths, a dysfunctional family of eccentric and borderline insane individuals who find the wealth that facilitates their spoiled lifestyles suddenly evaporate when the family patriarch and successful businessman George Bluth Sr. ( Jeffrey Tambor ) is imprisoned for fraud. Responsibility for managing the family falls to Michael Bluth ( Jason Bateman ), the only sensible member of the family, whose efforts to do the right thing and keep everyone united usually face obstacles in the form of his relatives’ materialistic, selfish, and juvenile ways. Where the first three seasons operated with a sense of lovable redemption for the miscreant mob, Arrested Development ’s two revivals had a crueler, more cutting nature. While it was a minor issue in Season 4, the shift became overbearing in the fifth and final season of the series, conjuring not only a greater sense of moral depravity through its emphasis on the characters’ unedifying flaws, but an unfortunate whiff of curt joylessness as well. The series always flaunted a certain irreverence, but Arrested Development Season 5 overplays its hand, presumably in an effort to remain fresh and surprising, but it only succeeds in losing the magic of its earlier seasons, creating an unrecognizable and unrewarding mess from what was once a razor-sharp comedy . 4 \'Fleabag\' (2016–2019) Phoebe Waller-Bridge staring into the camera while sitting in a pew in \'Fleabag\' Season 2. Image via Prime Video Given Fleabag consists of just two seasons and twelve episodes in total, it is staggering to fathom the scale of the cultural impact it has had. It is also quite perplexing to consider how the series changes quite substantially from Season 1 to Season 2 while remaining true to its core values and still delivering on the absorbing balance of razor-sharp comedy targeting everyday life and the underlying drama and despair of the titular character. The British comedy-drama follows a dry-witted and depressed woman known only as Fleabag ( Phoebe Waller-Bridge ) as she navigates life and love in the whirlwind that is modern-day London, as she struggles to overcome her feelings of grief and guilt regarding the death of her best friend, all while distancing herself from anyone who tries to help her process her emotions. While both seasons maintain plenty of comedy and drama, Season 2 is noticeably darker, delving into Fleabag’s complex emotional journey with a greater sense of urgency and honesty as she gradually grows beyond her despair as her unlikely friendship with the Hot Priest ( Andrew Scott ) starts to materialize into love. The season’s increased bleakness is a wonderful byproduct of its greater depth . It builds upon the richness of the first season magnificently to deliver a resolution to the story that is bittersweet but gorgeously cathartic. As both star and screenwriter, Waller-Bridge makes it work phenomenally, creating a series of unbelievable emotional range—given its relatively brief run—that stands as one of the defining small-screen triumphs of the 2010s , and an astute marriage of comedy and drama that is truly flawless from start to finish. 3 \'M*A*S*H\' (1972–1983) The M*A*S*H crew hugging and saying goodbye in the final episode, "Goodbye, Farewell and Amen" Image via CBS One of the more iconic series, not only in the context of comedy television but in the history of small-screen entertainment, M*A*S*H famously follows the medics at a Mobile Army Surgical Hospital during the Korean War, exhibiting how they use humor as a coping mechanism as they confront the horrific effects of battle. Based on Robert Altman ’s black comedy film of the same name from 1970, the hit series was never shy of using its wartime setting to address the severity of conflict, and it even has several episodes that are famous for their upsetting lulls. The last season, however, showcases a greater commitment to examining the brutality of war and pivots from outright comedy to a more concentrated war weariness at times as a result. Perhaps the best instance of this comes in the series’ finale, “Goodbye, Farewell, and Amen,” as the usually irreverent jokester Hawkeye Pierce ( Alan Alda ), being treated in a psychiatric hospital following a nervous breakdown, recalls an incident on a bus when his insistence that a refugee keeps her baby quiet to avoid detection from an enemy patrol leads to her smothering her child. It is a harrowing passage that illustrates how much bolder and bleaker the series was willing to go compared to the earlier seasons of its 11-season run. The increased drama is widely regarded to be a masterstroke, one that ensured M*A*S*H remained dynamic throughout all of its 256 episodes right up until its glorious two-hour finale that remains the most-watched single episode of any series in America. 2 \'Barry\' (2018–2023) A stressed and dejected looking Barry Berkman (Bill Hader) stands in a black t-shirt in \'Barry\' (2018-2023). HBO As a black comedy crime show following Barry Berkman ( Bill Hader ), a former U.S. Marine suffering from PTSD, as he finds an unlikely passion for acting while working as a hitman, Barry always flaunted a healthy dose of dramatic heft throughout its first three seasons, even if its beginnings are renowned more for their unique comical premise rather than their philosophical ponderings. The series did become increasingly dark as it went on, though, with Hader and co-creator Alec Berg becoming bolder at experimenting with the reliable mixture of dark humor and ultra-violence by introducing whiffs of real human drama to the fold. This balancing act takes a distinct elevation in intensity in Barry’s fourth and final season, with Barry in prison for murder and working to broker a deal with the FBI to work as an informant in exchange for a reduced sentence. The endearing quirkiness of Barry ’s situation in earlier seasons evaporates, with Season 4 committing to realizing the character as a vicious and volatile vessel of self-loathing whose outbursts of extreme violence are treated with an enhanced dramatic brutality compared to the absurdist, morbidly comical slant his actions were presented with in prior seasons. The unexpected tonal shift wasn’t necessarily met with universal appreciation from the fanbase, many of whom felt the show’s drastic change of mood correlated with weaker writing and less impactful narratives, but critics welcomed the evolution of the story as a daring way to wrap up the series. 1 \'BoJack Horseman\' (2014–2020) A scruffy and weathered looking BoJack Horseman stands on a bridge at night, the full moon serving as his backdrop as he talks on the phone in \'BoJack Horseman\' (2014-2020). Netflix Not dissimilar to Barry , BoJack Horseman is a series that always toed the line between laugh-out-loud hysterics and poignant, blindsiding drama. The groundbreaking Netflix adult animation follows BoJack Horseman ( Will Arnett ), a television actor who made his name in a hit family sitcom in the \'90s, who has since fallen into a cyclical lifestyle of addiction, self-loathing, and dreams of a second chance in the limelight while living as a washed-up celebrity in Los Angeles. Between attempts to launch a career comeback that will garner him artistic accolades and self-destructive benders that dismantle his chances of happiness and success, BoJack’s tendency to make mistakes and irrational decisions that harm those around him, a point that becomes painfully relevant in the series’ sixth season. Regret, consequences, and the lingering effects of trauma all become focal points of the final season, and while many would rightfully argue that those themes had been prevalent since the beginning of BoJack Horseman , the final episodes’ endeavor to address them more directly ensures the series takes on a distinctly different tone than its earlier seasons. It is an evolution that is handled magnificently, with the series’ darkening tone coinciding with BoJack’s long-standing internal turmoils surfacing in the most devastating and humiliating ways possible. The comedy, while still outrageously absurd, is steeped in tragedy . The tonal shift is instrumental in setting up what is one of the greatest and most contemplative series finales of all time. bojack-horseman-poster.jpg Like Follow Followed BoJack Horseman Drama Animation Comedy Release Date 2014 - 2020-00-00 Network Netflix Cast See All Amy Sedaris Will Arnett Where to watch Close WHERE TO WATCH Streaming Showrunner Raphael Bob-Waksberg Genres Drama , Animation , Comedy Powered by Expand Collapse Google is updating how content is shown. "/> ‘Fleabag’ is a reminder that love will pass, probably Katie Hulse | Staff Katie Hulse Author email Nov 6, 2025 Nov 6, 2025 Comments Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Chloe Kim | Senior Staff Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Love is heavy. Like an excruciating mound of weight on your back. A million pounds that you lug around that, as you try to heave it off the ground, inevitably drags you back toward it. It is embarrassing and horrific and also universally coveted. As I have been revisiting the concept of “art as a time machine” every week, it feels pointless to write about art without confronting the difficult truth that love is its most relentless subject matter. It seems to be indubitably trivial to study the way that time changes media without exploring how love changes art. “Fleabag,” created by, written by and starring Phoebe Waller-Bridge, is a piece of art that changed for me after I underwent the humiliation ritual of falling in love. I used to carefully strain out the cheesy, tasteless art in my life, sculpting a fortress of highbrow media around myself. But it’s been dreadful to learn that when you’re in love — like, really in love — you forget about your highbrow standards. The songs no longer make me wince; instead, they make sense. The rain falls quieter. Clothes are lighter on your skin, and then, as you allow yourself closer to the storm of love, they hang heavy and drenched. I used to spend my life wielding umbrellas and waterproof jackets to protect myself from the torrents of love. But now, I find myself bare in its downpour. I take delight in those cheesy songs. And for the first time, I understand overdone proclamations of love in movies and TV shows. “Fleabag”has been one of my favorite TV shows for years — long before love — despite being the antithesis to any romantic feeling. In its second season, it is a love story between the main character, Fleabag, (Phoebe Waller-Bridge) and a priest. It is dry, witty, pessimistic and always waiting rabidly to harshly remind me: My emotions are mortal. At the climax of the story, the priest makes a speech at a wedding. I’ve always regarded it as merely beautiful and fitting, maybe a little overly mushy and most definitely not the truth. Now, I feel I have the privilege of understanding it fully. My father likes to watch this episode after anything disturbing or scary. He sees it as a return to humanity, or something like that. On my most recent rewatch with my family, I devoured the wedding speech in a way that was impossible before the relationship that I’m in now. In a way that helped me accept that love is agonizing but apparently worth feeling. The priest’s famous lines read, “It makes you doubt yourself, judge yourself, distance yourself from the other people in your life. It makes you selfish. It makes you creepy, makes you obsessed with your hair, makes you cruel, makes you say and do things you never thought you would do. It’s all any of us want, and it’s hell when we get there.” And while I do believe love is all of these things, I never thought it would make me see art so differently. A nourishing relationship comes with so many little sacrifices. These small forfeits accumulate quietly. Love isn’t just a feeling; it’s a commodity. It has invented value, and just like everything else, it does not come free. Emotional highs and lows drive some kind of invisible stock of connection. At love’s most fundamental, when you allow someone to get to know you, you’re eradicating the version of yourself that others once could know. And when you love that someone knows you so well, you shut out the rest of the world. But honestly, I would be lying if I tried to say love is something that could be logically measured or placed on a scale. Its value derives from its sickening irrationality, and when real decisions are forced upon love, sacrifices are often an afterthought. In “Fleabag,” the priest chronically sacrifices his religious beliefs for his opportunity at love. And in the end, the cost is too high. Abandoning our main character at a bus stop post-one-sided-love-confession, he promises Fleabag, “It’ll pass.” The phrase triumphs as the famous romantic certainty of the series: that love is all-consuming but also beatable. There are many versions of love and many places to invest it. The priest decides to invest his in religion. Whether due to religious responsibilities or predestined distance, people in love, at one time or another, must be forced to confront the unknown value of their relationship — forced to decide what exactly they are willing to sacrifice to sustain it. My significant other is, unfortunately, also my best friend. Soon, I will be forced to make impossible decisions about my illogical feelings. I am going to graduate and he is moving abroad. While we spend our days numbed by our own happiness, reality’s ugly head is already rearing. And while the dilemma is perhaps small, it feels bigger than any piece of art or media can solve. The concept of measuring relationships is something that has been weighing on my mind. I have been desperately attempting to be rational, to gain confidence in my malleability, attempting to fit something incomprehensible into a pros and cons list. And from an unbiased scribble of reason, it does not make sense to hold onto something as youthful, naive and content as my relationship. I keep telling myself that I could be anywhere in a year, while he remains here or somewhere else corrupting his soul in investment banking. Why would I want to stay with anyone in investment banking? Yet for some reason, I keep thinking about the line that Fleabag’s sister, Claire, says to Fleabag after the priest’s speech. She says, “The only person I’d run through an airport for is you.” But right after saying it, Claire chases someone else through an airport. Time is the only measurement slightly worthwhile to my relationship, but that’s only because I think that love itself is predicated on time. Some people spend it making art, and others spend it running through airports. Graham Norton has said he is “delighted” to be the newest ambassador for the Edinburgh Festival Fringe – where he started his career as a comedian more than 30 years ago. The television presenter, author and comedian takes on the role alongside previously announced ambassadors Brian Cox, Suzy Eddie Izzard and the Fringe Society’s honorary president, Phoebe Waller-Bridge. Norton’s connection with the Fringe dates back to 1991 when he was honing his craft as a stand-up, performing Mother Teresa Of Calcutta’s Grand Farewell Tour in the Pleasance Attic, a newly opened 60-seat venue at the Pleasance. He went on to work in television, including appearing as priest Father Noel in Father Ted, while continuing to perform at the Fringe, where he was shortlisted for the Perrier Award in 1997. His chat show The Graham Norton Show launched in 2007 on the BBC and has featured a host of stars including Taylor Swift, who recently gave her first TV interview to Norton on the day of the release of her latest album The Life Of A Showgirl. Commenting on his appointment as Fringe ambassador, Norton said: “It’s hard to believe that my connection to the Edinburgh Festival Fringe dates back nearly 35 years. “As an emerging comedian back in the early 90s, everyone in the industry knew that you had to make the journey to Edinburgh and its Fringe for the opportunities that you have to develop your craft with a live audience, but also to meet and network with the thousands from the industry that go there to look for talent. “Through my chat show I meet and talk to those across the entertainment industry every week, and you’d be hard-pressed to find someone on the sofa that hasn’t been to the Fringe – either to perform or to watch shows at some point in the past. “I’m delighted to be announced as an ambassador of the Edinburgh Fringe and look forward to visiting the festival next August.” Norton’s connection with the Edinburgh Fringe dates back more than three decades (Brian Lawless/PA) Norton returns to Edinburgh most summers to watch shows at the Fringe and support friends. He is the author of several novels and hosts the podcast Wanging On with Maria McErlane. Tony Lankester, chief executive of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society, said: “Our ambassadors represent the critical role the Fringe plays in the lives of so many who got their start on the stages of Edinburgh and, today, are at the top of their game in the world of the arts. “Welcoming Graham to the fold is a real pleasure – he is someone who exemplifies the joy and generosity of the Fringe spirit, unapologetically passionate about the arts and a huge advocate of the importance of the Fringe in his own career. “As an ambassador he will be uniquely positioned to help inspire the next generation of artists, and we’re excited to be working with him on this mission.” The Edinburgh Festival Fringe will run from August 7 to 31 next year. Tony Lankester, chief executive of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society, said: “Our ambassadors represent the critical role the Fringe plays in the lives of so many who got their start on the stages of Edinburgh and, today, are at the top of their game in the world of the arts. “Welcoming Graham to the fold is a real pleasure – he is someone who exemplifies the joy and generosity of the Fringe spirit, unapologetically passionate about the arts and a huge advocate of the importance of the Fringe in his own career. “As an ambassador he will be uniquely positioned to help inspire the next generation of artists, and we’re excited to be working with him on this mission.” The Edinburgh Festival Fringe will run from August 7 to 31 next year. Martin Teases "I\'m not developing them alone." Several more Game of Thrones spinoff projects remain in development, creator George R.R. Martin has teased, including "some sequels." Yesterday, HBO laid out a Marvel-style slate for the future of the Game of Thrones universe , and confirmed multiple upcoming seasons for both House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms due for release over the next three years. Beyond those two shows, however, Martin has confirmed he\'s helping develop even more projects that are officially "in development" — including plans for multiple series set after Game of Thrones\' controversial finale. "Aside from The Knight of the Seven Kingdoms and House of the Dragon, there are other Game of Thrones spinoff projects in development," Martin said at an event attended by Los Siete Reinos . "Most are prequels. There are several in development, five or six series; and I\'m not developing them alone, I\'m working with other people. Yes, there are some sequels." Of course, both of HBO\'s current Game of Thrones spinoffs are prequels, with House of the Dragon set two centuries before the events of its parent show. A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is set roughly within the middle of the two, taking place around 100 years before. Martin has previously discussed other potential spinoff ideas, including an Aegon the Conqueror show (around 300 years pre-Game of Thrones), a scrapped series centering on warrior queen Nymeria (who lived 1,000 years in the past), and yet another abandoned idea, entitled 10,000 Ships, which would have focused on a sea-faring city . House of the Dragon Season 3 Cast and Characters: Who’s New and Who’s Returning? View 28 Images At the same time, the author has been more coy over plans for anything set after Game of Thrones\' end — something he\'s still two books away from reaching himself. Warning! Spoilers for Game of Thrones follow: While Game of Thrones\' final season is something of a bloodbath, numerous fan-favorite characters remain alive at its end — leaving the door open to several potential follow-ups. Indeed, Jon Snow actor Kit Harington previously confirmed he\'d had discussions about returning for his own spinoff, though the idea was shelved after "a couple of years back and forth developing it." Maisie Williams. Image credit: Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic via Getty Images. Fans have long hoped for more from Arya Stark, last seen sailing off into the horizon in search of fresh adventures. Last December, Martin even mentioned a meeting between himself and actress Maisie Williams , and teased something as being in the works. "We also got together with Maisie Williams for pizza and pasta, and talked about... Well, no, better not get into that, do not want to jinx it," Martin said. "But it could be so much fun." Of course, it\'s worth stressing that countless TV shows described as being in some stage of "development" never actually make it on-screen. The author shared the update during a session at the 2025 Iceland Noir Festival, according to international media reports. Martin did not specify whether the sequels would be television series or feature films, but noted that he is developing the new titles with multiple collaborators rather than writing alone. The revelation has reignited long-standing speculation about an Arya Stark follow-up. Maisie Williams\'s character sailed west of Westeros in the much-debated Season 8 finale — a storyline fans have frequently cited as ripe for further exploration. The original "Game of Thrones", adapted from Martin\'s "A Song of Ice and Fire" novels, premiered in 2011 and quickly became one of HBO\'s defining global hits. Spanning Westeros and Essos, the series charted power struggles for the Iron Throne, Daenerys Targaryen\'s quest to reclaim her family\'s legacy, and the Night\'s Watch facing threats from beyond the Wall. Los Angeles, Nov 1 (IANS) Taking a leaf out of her 1998 romantic comedy film, actress Nicole Kidman added "just a little bit" of "Perfect Magic" to her 2025 Halloween celebration. Kidman took to Instagram, where she shared a series of nature-themed tarot cards. "Just a little #PracticalMagic for your Halloween," the Practical Magic star captioned the post, seemingly teasing the 1998 film\'s upcoming sequel. The cards pictured in the post feature detailed illustrations of an oak tree, an acorn, a bowl of salt, the sun and several flowers. The cards were photographed among lavender bushes and daisies. The last slide of the post included two of the cards on a candlelit table alongside a sketch pad featuring the draft illustrations next to pressed flowers, reports people.com. "Practical Magic" is a romantic fantasy film based on the 1995 novel by Alice Hoffman. The film was directed by Griffin Dunne and stars Sandra Bullock, Nicole Kidman, Dianne Wiest, Stockard Channing and Aidan Quinn. Bullock and Kidman play sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, descended from a long line of witches. Kidman will be reprising her role as Gillian Owens in the Halloween favorite\'s sequel. Stockard Channing and Dianne Wiest are also set to reprise their roles as the eclectic aunts of Sally Owens and Gillian. Channing will once again play Frances "Franny" Owens, the more no-nonsense of the pair, while Wiest returns as the kind, whimsical, understanding Bridget "Jet" Owens, read an official release. New additions to the cast in the follow-up to the iconic witchy romance are Joey King as Sally\'s daughter, plus Lee Pace, Maisie Williams, Xolo Mariduena and Solly McLeod. In a statement earlier this year, the filmmaking team behind Practical Magic 2, which includes director Susanne Bier, taking over from Griffin Dunne, said, "Twenty-five years ago, Sally, Gillian, Aunt Jet and Aunt Franny flew off the pages of Alice Hoffman\'s beloved novel and into theaters around the world, and we are thrilled to bring the Owens family back to the big screen with Joey, Lee, Maisie, Solly and Xolo joining the next chapter in our story." Martin Teases "I\'m not developing them alone." Several more Game of Thrones spinoff projects remain in development, creator George R.R. Martin has teased, including "some sequels." Yesterday, HBO laid out a Marvel-style slate for the future of the Game of Thrones universe , and confirmed multiple upcoming seasons for both House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms due for release over the next three years. Beyond those two shows, however, Martin has confirmed he\'s helping develop even more projects that are officially "in development" — including plans for multiple series set after Game of Thrones\' controversial finale. "Aside from The Knight of the Seven Kingdoms and House of the Dragon, there are other Game of Thrones spinoff projects in development," Martin said at an event attended by Los Siete Reinos . "Most are prequels. There are several in development, five or six series; and I\'m not developing them alone, I\'m working with other people. Yes, there are some sequels." Of course, both of HBO\'s current Game of Thrones spinoffs are prequels, with House of the Dragon set two centuries before the events of its parent show. A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is set roughly within the middle of the two, taking place around 100 years before. Martin has previously discussed other potential spinoff ideas, including an Aegon the Conqueror show (around 300 years pre-Game of Thrones), a scrapped series centering on warrior queen Nymeria (who lived 1,000 years in the past), and yet another abandoned idea, entitled 10,000 Ships, which would have focused on a sea-faring city . House of the Dragon Season 3 Cast and Characters: Who’s New and Who’s Returning? View 28 Images At the same time, the author has been more coy over plans for anything set after Game of Thrones\' end — something he\'s still two books away from reaching himself. Warning! Spoilers for Game of Thrones follow: While Game of Thrones\' final season is something of a bloodbath, numerous fan-favorite characters remain alive at its end — leaving the door open to several potential follow-ups. Indeed, Jon Snow actor Kit Harington previously confirmed he\'d had discussions about returning for his own spinoff, though the idea was shelved after "a couple of years back and forth developing it." Maisie Williams. Image credit: Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic via Getty Images. Fans have long hoped for more from Arya Stark, last seen sailing off into the horizon in search of fresh adventures. Last December, Martin even mentioned a meeting between himself and actress Maisie Williams , and teased something as being in the works. "We also got together with Maisie Williams for pizza and pasta, and talked about... Well, no, better not get into that, do not want to jinx it," Martin said. "But it could be so much fun." Of course, it\'s worth stressing that countless TV shows described as being in some stage of "development" never actually make it on-screen. Martin has previously confirmed that three animated shows set in the same universe are also in development, signalling HBO\'s long-term commitment to expanding the franchise. Los Angeles, Nov 1 (IANS) Taking a leaf out of her 1998 romantic comedy film, actress Nicole Kidman added "just a little bit" of "Perfect Magic" to her 2025 Halloween celebration. Kidman took to Instagram, where she shared a series of nature-themed tarot cards. "Just a little #PracticalMagic for your Halloween," the Practical Magic star captioned the post, seemingly teasing the 1998 film\'s upcoming sequel. The cards pictured in the post feature detailed illustrations of an oak tree, an acorn, a bowl of salt, the sun and several flowers. The cards were photographed among lavender bushes and daisies. The last slide of the post included two of the cards on a candlelit table alongside a sketch pad featuring the draft illustrations next to pressed flowers, reports people.com. "Practical Magic" is a romantic fantasy film based on the 1995 novel by Alice Hoffman. The film was directed by Griffin Dunne and stars Sandra Bullock, Nicole Kidman, Dianne Wiest, Stockard Channing and Aidan Quinn. Bullock and Kidman play sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, descended from a long line of witches. Kidman will be reprising her role as Gillian Owens in the Halloween favorite\'s sequel. Stockard Channing and Dianne Wiest are also set to reprise their roles as the eclectic aunts of Sally Owens and Gillian. Channing will once again play Frances "Franny" Owens, the more no-nonsense of the pair, while Wiest returns as the kind, whimsical, understanding Bridget "Jet" Owens, read an official release. New additions to the cast in the follow-up to the iconic witchy romance are Joey King as Sally\'s daughter, plus Lee Pace, Maisie Williams, Xolo Mariduena and Solly McLeod. In a statement earlier this year, the filmmaking team behind Practical Magic 2, which includes director Susanne Bier, taking over from Griffin Dunne, said, "Twenty-five years ago, Sally, Gillian, Aunt Jet and Aunt Franny flew off the pages of Alice Hoffman\'s beloved novel and into theaters around the world, and we are thrilled to bring the Owens family back to the big screen with Joey, Lee, Maisie, Solly and Xolo joining the next chapter in our story." Credit: Nicole Kidman / Instagram Nicole Kidman, Ariana Grande interview has unexpectedly given fans insight into Keith Urban marriage breakdown Madeline Cove The Nightly 25 November 2025, 6:40am Copy link Share story Nicole Kidman has offered the first real glimpse into how she is coping after the collapse of her 18-year marriage to Keith Urban, and her understated answer says more than any statement could. In a new Interview Magazine profile on Ariana Grande, Kidman briefly slips out from behind the interviewer’s role when Grande asks how she is. Kidman replies simply, “I’m hanging in there”. It’s the clearest signal yet of the emotional toll following the couple’s shock split, finalised just weeks after reports emerged they had quietly separated months earlier. The exchange took place over Zoom, with Kidman dialling in from Nashville, the city where she and Urban raised daughters Sunday and Faith, and Grande speaking from New York. Despite the upheaval, Kidman’s affection for Wicked is undimmed. She recalled seeing the first film with her girls, booking an entire row at a Nashville cinema. Entertainment Keith Urban dropped massive divorce hint weeks before split The Nightly Nicole Kidman ‘arrested’ at concert as viral video emerges “When I saw Wicked with my girls, we actually booked out the whole row here in Nashville and it was just crazy,” she said. “People were cheering, and it was just really, really fun. So that was exciting, right? For that to take off.” Kidman also touched on returning to witchcraft, onscreen at least, for the sequel to Practical Magic. Filming wrapped in London between July and September, just before her separation from Urban became public. She admitted the timing could have been devastating, but instead, she said the woman-led cast shielded her. “Sandy Bullock and I, and then Joey King and Maisie (Williams)– we had an incredible cast. A lot of times I don’t have fun when I’m filming... But I have such a strong relationship with all those women, so I felt protected and loved. Loading Instagram Post “It was just very, very safe.” Kidman and Grande also bonded over their favourite form of self-care, which was ending the night in the bath. “That’s my sanctuary. I love talking on the phone (in the bath),” Kidman said. Court filings later confirmed the Lioness star has filed for divorce, citing “irreconcilable differences” and was named the primary parent of the couple’s teenage daughters. Kidman has maintained a public presence since, appearing at events in Dallas and Paris — even debuting freshly cut “break-up bangs” backstage at Fashion Week. Not a year goes by that a new season of a popular show doesn’t land on the Paramount+ streaming service and take the world by storm. However, the movie side of Star Trek can’t seem to get things right. Quentin Tarantino threw his hat in the ring, wanting to develop a project in the universe that means so much to him. Unfortunately, the whole thing fell apart, and so has every other attempt to bring the Enterprise back to the big screen. Recent reports even claim that Paramount is giving up on bringing Chris Pine and the rest of his crew back for one last ride. Videos by ComicBook.com Losing the Kelvin Timeline will be a tough pill to swallow, since all the recent shows owe their existence to it. It’s hard to imagine a world where Star Trek is as big as it is right now if J.J. Abrams hadn’t taken that swing in 2009. But living in the past isn’t healthy, so it’s time to look toward the future. Here are seven actors who would be perfect as the original Enterprise crew in the next Star Trek movie reboot. 7) Ivanna Sakhno as Pavel Chekov Even if the Kelvin Timeline actors returned, there would be a massive void, as Pavel Chekov actor Anton Yelchin tragically lost his life shortly before the release of Star Trek Beyond . Anyone looking to fill his shoes will need to take things in a totally different direction, and Ivanna Sakhno is the person for the job. In Star Wars: Ahsoka, her role is that of a bright Force-user named Shin Hati, who loses her way and joins forces with Baylan Skoll. There’s an edge to Hati that Sakhno can bring to Chekov, turning the character from a lovable know-it-all into someone who understands that the hard choices are sometimes the right ones. 6) Mackenyu as Hikaru Sulu Despite having limited screen time, John Cho delivers a masterful performance as Hikaru Sulu, the helmsman of the Enterprise. He keeps the crew grounded, always being willing to offer advice to those who need it, but he’s also not afraid to take matters into his own hands if the situation calls for it. An actor who excels at stepping up in big moments is Mackenyu, best known for his work in live-action manga adaptations in JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Diamond Is Unbreakable – Chapter 1 . In Netflix’s One Piece , he betrays pirate hunter Roronoa Zoro, who may not seem like he has much in common with Sulu. However, they will both do anything to keep their friends safe, even if it costs them their lives. 5) Jaz Sinclair as Nyota Uhura There aren’t many franchises left for Zoe Saldaña to conquer. She appears in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, and James Cameron’s Avatar franchise. But her best performance might be in the Star Trek trilogy, where she portrays Nyota Uhura, a communications officer. While it’s going to be tough to replace Saldaña, one name on the rise that fits Uhura’s strong personality is Jaz Sinclair, star of The Boys spinoff Gen V . Her character, Marie Moreau, has more potential than her classmates , which screams Uhura, and she’s never afraid to call out her friends when she thinks they’re making bad decisions. 4) Jack Lowden as Montgomery “Scotty” Scott The best aspect of Scotty’s character is that he’s loyal, sometimes to a fault. He trusts the people in charge and is ready to put his life on the line for them. However, Scotty isn’t perfect, as he’s been known to drop the ball from time to time. If there’s one other character that fits that description, it’s River Cartwright from Apple TV+’s Slow Horses . Jack Lowden’s character constantly puts himself in ridiculous situations, but he always finds a way to come out on top. Scotty could use an extra bit of luck going into the next movie, and Lowden can provide it. Read Next Star Trek’s Boldest Ship Redesign Happened Completely By Accident 3) Cooper Hoffman as Leonard “Bones” McCoy Bones is a lot like Scotty, but he’s going to complain more than his shippmate. He has every reason to, though, as the fate of every member of the crew is in his hands, since he’s the ship’s doctor. But despite all the stress, Bones can always elicit a laugh when he needs to. The Long Walk places Cooper Hoffman in an incredibly stressful situation , having his character, Ray Garraty, walk alongside dozens of other young men in an attempt to win riches. Falling behind means death, so Garraty tries to keep spirits high as the journey continues. Hoffman can do the same thing as Scotty whenever a new alien threat starts shooting at the Enterprise . 2) Asa Butterfield as Spock When Zachary Quinto landed the role of Spock in Abrams’ Star Trek , people didn’t expect much because they thought it would be impossible for anyone to pick up the baton from Leonard Nimoy. Well, Quinto proved the haters wrong, turning in standout performances in all three of his Star Trek appearances. Finding a replacement for Quinto might be even more challenging than finding one for Nimoy, but the powers that be should give Asa Butterfield the first crack at it. The Sex Education actor knows how to play characters who struggle with social situations, and he won’t ever have a problem sounding like the most intelligent person in the room. 1) David Jonsson as James T. Kirk Of course, the most important character in any Star Trek movie about the original crew is James T. Kirk, the captain of the Enterprise. His trademark move is pushing back against authority, and not just any actor can pull it off. Someone with real range needs to bring Kirk to life. Fortunately, one actor on the rise has the makings of a great captain. Hoffman’s co-star in The Long Walk , David Jonnson, typically has a calming presence, rallying those around him to be better versions of themselves. However, he can turn up the dial when he needs to, as his performance in Alien: Romulus proves. Bringing Jonsson into the fold would give the next Star Trek movie instant credibility, as he’s quickly becoming one of the best actors of his generation. What do you think? Read more Jimmy Cliff remembered: The reggae artist’s most important music Read more November 10, 2025 6:30 am Share Share on Facebook Post google Google Preferred Pin it Show more sharing options Share to Flipboard Post to Tumblr Submit to Reddit Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Email Print This Page 0 Few people can claim to have as much of a bottom-to-top understanding of how a set works quite like Gen V director and executive producer Steve Boyum . Having started out working in stunts, Boyum cut his teeth movies like Apocalypse Now , The Blues Brothers , and Predator before transitioning to second unit directing and eventually directing. And that climb up the ladder shapes how to views the job. "Directing, to me, is reacting," Boyum told Gold Derby during our "Meet the Experts: Spotlight" interview series with TV directors. "If I\'m working with a showrunner, we\'re designing a series. But what I\'ve learned over the years is that actors are bringing something that they\'ve prepared, and they\'ve studied this character. The cameraman has an idea of what he wants to do visually. Everybody loves what they\'re doing, and they can bring things that, as a director and a producer, you\'re reacting to. I look at directing and filmmaking as, a paintbrush in someone\'s hand. There\'s 500 bristles on a brush." Related Stories Building the emotional architecture of ‘Hamnet’: An exclusive look at the Shakespearean production design 2026 Grammys Best Rap lineup shows that rumors of hip-hop’s death are greatly exaggerated One of the more recent examples of that kind of collaboration arose during production on Season 2 of The Boys spinoff. Hamish Linklater had joined the cast as Dean Cipher and brought something to the role that even showrunner Michele Fazekas hadn\'t even foreseen. "When we cast Hamish Linklater in Season 2 to be Cipher, Michele had written this character, and I\'d looked at it on the page in all the different ways," Boyum said. "I knew Hamish as Abraham Lincoln [in Manhunt ], and he turns up on the set and he brings this interpretation that I kid you not, nobody in the world could have anticipated what this was other than Hamish. Completely at odds with everything that Michele and I never envisioned it to be, but probably 10 times better ultimately. And then [series lead] Jaz Sinclair is in the scene with him. And I\'m watching her watch him and she\'s like, holy sh-t." It was that element of surprise that put Linklater\'s collaborators back on their heels and forced them to view their own work differently and, according to Boyum, for the better. "So Hamish\'s interpretation of this character took Jaz to a place that she hadn\'t really thought to go," he said. "You get swept up with each other making film. It\'s such a great collaboration." Audiences have seen some exceptionally nasty things play out in the universe of The Boys , as supes have a tendency to get up to some super gross behavior. Between both The Boys and Gen V , the canon has featured all varieties of deviant behavior, be it violent, sexual, or… other. It makes one wonder how the bar can be raised even higher, and in the case of Gen V , I’m keeping my fingers tightly crossed for a Season 3 so that the show can find a way to top the season’s gnarliest moment from the Season 2 finale . In the last episode of Gen V , our heroes must find some way to stop the even Thomas Godolkin (Ethan Slater), who has decided that supe standards have become too loose, and he hopes to “cull” the majority of the population at Godolkin University. Stopping him means getting into the training facility where he is secretly inviting students to be slaughtered – but the protagonists can’t just stroll in. So what do they do? The majority of them hide within the special, infinitely cavernous anus of Black Hole (Wyatt Dorion), and they emerge to fight when the time is right. It’s a moment that now lives as an all-timer highlight in the Boys continuity, and the stars of the show all talked about it giddily when I interviewed them about the show this fall. It Was More Than Expected As captured in the video at the top of this article, I sat down with stars Jaz Sinclair, London Thor, Derek Luh, Lizze Broadway, Maddie Phillips, Asa Germann, Sean Patrick Thomas and Hamish Linklater a few weeks ago during the Los Angeles press day for Gen V Season 2, and one question I asked all of them was about their experience executing the finale’s big twist. They all most definitely acknowledge it as one of the wildest things to ever play out in either Gen V or The Boys , and they were wowed by just the sheer creativeness of it. Said Thomas, I mean, my impression is like, 'Goddamn that's genius.' That's my impression. I mean, who would think of that? Yeah. And it's not just like a silly gag. It's for a purpose. It's to help. More Gen V! ‘Man, Was I Sweating It’: Gen V Executes An Amazing Surprise For Hamish Linklater In Season 2’s Final Episodes, And The Actor Loved It, But It Freaked Him Out -- ‘It Is Very Creepy’: Gen V's Hamish Linklater And Sean Patrick Thomas Dig Into Cipher’s Nightmarish Puppeteering Of Polarity What makes the moment so great is the fact that it’s not really just a random idea or joke. Black Hole and his special anal cavity are featured in Gen V Season 2 right from the start of the run – though you are just meant to think initially that he is just one of the show’s many strange background/supporting characters. But no: there is a special reason why the show introduces the idea of an infinite anus, and it’s to execute what I think can fairly be called the most disgusting Trojan Horse gambit in the history of television. As for the actual execution of the scene on set, the stars explained that the filmmakers executed some special craft to make the moment happen. There was not only a “slide” for the actors to go on to simulate their exit, but there was also a “fake butt” for them to emerge from. London Thor (who plays Jordan Li along with Derek Luh) explained that shooting it definitely wasn’t without its awkwardness: It was a fake butt. It was a butt. 'Cause we had to touch it. I had to put my hand on it and like push myself out. I saw that, and the intimacy coordinator had to come up to me, she's like, 'We didn't discuss this. I didn't know this is, are you good?' I'm like, 'I guess.' [Laughs] Not gonna say no. It's just a plastic butt. But yeah, that was rough . That was a hard to do experience. It was hard to watch. It’s nasty business, for sure – but it’s also now a scene that will forever be a highlight in the show’s legacy, and it’s a high bar that filmmakers will have to reach for as the canon continues to expand. Gen V Season 3 hasn’t gotten the green light yet (fingers are tightly crossed), but The Boys Season 5 is coming in 2026 , and also on the way is the new prequel series Vought Rising starring Jensen Ackles and Aya Cash.
